clinician.trajectory_summary: A 35-year-old male oil palm plantation worker presented with a 2-year progressive verrucous plaque on the buttocks, thigh, and scrotum that began as small mildly pruritic plaques and progressed over the last 5 months with painful itchy nodules, ulceration, and foul-smelling seropurulent discharge. He also reported untreated cough and night sweats for 2 years. Prior antifungal and antibiotic therapy had failed. Physical examination revealed an extensive verrucous plaque with dark dense crust, irregular border, fissures, multiple ulcers, and foul-smelling seropurulent discharge. Skin biopsy histopathology showed marked pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, epithelioid granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis, Langerhans cells, and lymphocytic infiltrates. AFB staining and mycobacterial culture were negative. Despite negative mycobacterial studies, the clinical presentation, typical histopathological findings, and occupational exposure supported the diagnosis of tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. Anti-tuberculous therapy (2-month intensive phase with RIPE followed by 4-month continuation phase with RH three times weekly) was initiated. At 2-month follow-up, skin lesions showed significant improvement, and by 4 months, lesions were completely resolved leaving only atrophic scars, confirming the diagnosis through treatment response.
